articles.title: New student reading data offer bright spot on long road to literacy recovery in the US
articles.summary: Reading scores are starting to see an increase across the board after years of stagnation following COVID-19, a new study says, a hopeful sign in the long battle to improve literacy among U.S. students. Reading scores in grades K through 8 cut the gap from pre-pandemic levels by one-third in the past year, according to…
articles.body:
Reading scores are starting to see an increase across the board after years of stagnation following COVID-19, a new study says, a hopeful sign in the long battle to improve literacy among U.S. students.

Reading scores in grades K through 8 cut the gap from pre-pandemic levels by one-third in the past year, according to data from NWEA, an education research group. While an encouraging sign that experts think can be attributed to some new reading policies implemented at the state level, more progress is needed before students get back to pre-COVID success rates.

“The kind of improvements we saw from 2025 to 2026, so this last year in reading, really stood out because we had seen such stagnation for the four years previously. It seemed like schools were doing lots of things, schools were back in, kind of to normal, but we weren’t seeing that any kind of real road to recovery on average,” said Megan Kuhfeld, director of Growth Modeling and Analytics at NWEA.

The scores “just kind of dropped and then stagnated. So, the fact that we saw these kind of small improvements, but still meaningful improvements over the last year, was really encouraging,” Kuhfeld added.

Experts believe the improvements are a sign that efforts by states to implement the science of reading and add more literacy tutoring were not in vain.

Since the pandemic, around half of states have adopted laws or requirements for schools to align their literacy teaching with the science of reading , a practice that focuses on phonics, the ability of students to sound out words and understanding how letters sound together. It also has a greater emphasis on vocabulary and comprehension.

The standard that lawmakers are increasingly tossed to the wayside is the balanced literacy approach, where students are encouraged to use “cues” to understand what they are reading, placing a greater emphasis on whole words over individual sounds.

“This is likely a reflection of what some state lawmakers have done to pay attention to that subject specifically,” said Jonathan Butcher, acting director of the Center for Education Policy at the Heritage Foundation.

The NWEA data showed the biggest improvements in the past year were among Black students, Hispanic students and those in high-poverty areas, aligning with the groups that saw the biggest hits to their reading scores during the pandemic.

But experts caution that such hopeful scores have in the past been followed by fluctuation.

“We’ve seen this before, where there’s period of growth and then we see a decline,” said Weadé James, senior director for K-12 Education Policy at the Center for American Progress, noting all the efforts districts were able to undertake with the extra COVID-19 relief funding.

Without the continuation of that funding, James wonders “how states can continue a lot of these efforts that they started.”

According to the NWEA data, there is still a two-thirds gap between where students are now in reading and where they were before the pandemic.

And while getting above pre-coronavirus numbers would be a huge achievement, it doesn’t solve the U.S.’s long-running literacy decline.

Reading scores were on the rise from the 1990s up until 2013, when a switch the Education Scorecard May 2026 report described as a “learning recess” began. The report notes that the slowdown occurred during the rise in social media.

The Nation’s Report Card found only 14 percent of 13-year-olds read for fun every day in 2025, compared to 27 percent in 2012.

“On the nation’s report card, you find sometimes that these improvements don’t stick, and I think that’s because what content is taught is really important as well. And I think that if these reading gains are to persist, I think we’ve got to focus on what students are being taught, not just the skill, because they’re teaching the skill, but it’s got to be followed with content,” Butcher said.

The 2025 Program for International Assessment, an international assessment of students’ reading, science and math scores in different countries, showed 15-year-olds in the U.S. saw their reading scores fall 14 points since the test was last administered in 2022.

Along with the continuation of the science of reading, experts want to see other initiatives from states and school districts, such as more tutoring, early literacy screening and high-quality instruction for teachers.

“We need to make sure we don’t have a fragmented system, that literacy should really be looking at the entirety of a child’s schooling, and those standards should be aligned to ensure that we’re actually delivering the best quality instruction, and kids have the skills that they need when they do complete their studies,” said James.

articles.title: Back to school in Gaza: Learning in tents after years of disruption
articles.summary: After nearly three years of disruption, children return to school in Gaza in makeshift spaces with scarce resources.
articles.body:
Gaza City – Early on Saturday morning, Rana Totah held her two sons’ hands as she walked them to school in al-Katiba, Gaza City, watching them return to a routine they had almost forgotten.

For Totah, 30, the morning was more than the first day of a new school year. It was a return to family life interrupted by nearly three years of war and displacement after Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.

Displaced from Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood to al-Katiba in western Gaza City, Totah spent the previous night preparing her children for their first day back in face-to-face education.

She made sure they slept early the night before, then woke them, dressed them and brought them to school.

“Honestly, today was a beautiful day for me. It even felt like Eid,” Totah told Al Jazeera. “I prepared my children, they were excited and they went to bed early. I prepared them as if it were a normal school day.”

The Gaza Municipality school was set up in about 10 tents in the western Gaza City neighbourhood as a temporary space for a return to face-to-face education. “Sometimes there would be months when I stopped taking them altogether,” Totah said.

During the war, including when the family was in Khan Younis, Totah tried to keep her four children in education through informal learning via volunteer-led initiatives. But attendance was irregular, with the dangers of war and the struggle to find necessities a priority for parents, teachers and students. Ultimately, survival came before school, and her children took on essential tasks such as fetching water, despite Totah’s pleas for them to focus on learning.

“There were very difficult days. They would think about things like, ‘Mum, bring me water,’ or ‘Mum, let me go and get you this.’ And I would tell them, ‘ No, I want to focus on your studies.’ Education is the foundation of everything in life.”

The return to face-to-face education comes after nearly three years of disruption due to Israel’s genocidal war, which has seen almost all of Gaza’s population displaced and most buildings in the enclave destroyed.

About 541,000 students returned to education in Gaza when the new school year began on September 19, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education, which comes after a decrease – but not an end – in violence following the October 2025 ceasefire.

In January, the ministry said 317,332 students were attending face-to-face educational spaces, schools and initiatives in Gaza. Another 120,000 were enrolled in virtual schools taught by teachers from the West Bank.

However, despite the Gaza ceasefire, Israeli bombing has continued, with two students killed earlier this month. Such dangers have severely affected the learning environment and education remains severely constrained by war and other realities on the ground.

Nearly 98 percent of school buildings in Gaza had been damaged since October 2023, with more than 93 percent requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, according to UNICEF.

About 700,000 children aged four to 17 had missed formal face-to-face schooling for almost three consecutive school years, with around 420,000 having no face-to-face learning at all.

Inside one tent, Nesma Nahid Abu Asim was teaching mathematics to sixth-grade students, writing on a whiteboard as children sat on mattresses with notebooks on their laps.

Abu Asim has been a maths teacher since 2010. She worked for the Ministry of Education before the war and now teaches through a UNICEF programme supporting education in Gaza.

“During this period, education has been very difficult. There have been major challenges for both parents and teachers as we try to get the student to safety,” she said.

“Education is a right for every student … [but] students arrive without basic stationery or textbooks, while tables and chairs are largely unavailable. The student comes to school today in a dangerous situation, in a war situation.”

Due to Israel’s ongoing siege on Gaza, schools have reported a severe lack of stationery, schoolbooks, desks, and chairs. But for Abu Asim, her biggest concern is the threat of another interruption to education.

“These conditions are difficult for the student, but they are not impossible conditions. The biggest difficulty is that we stop education,” she said.

“We have taken a good step and opened the school year. We are returning to normal life, to education. The student has the right to learn and to sit at a school desk.”

Now she hopes temporary classrooms will eventually give way to safer and more permanent spaces for Gaza City’s children.

“I hope the schools will be emptied of displaced families and returned to these students. These students are our children,” she said. “We cannot put 40 students in a tent. In a classroom, we can have 40 students.”

As his teacher continues her maths lesson, 11-year-old Osama Alayleh briefly paused to tell Al Jazeera how his first day in class feels. “I’m happy that I’m back at school,” he said.

Osama ranked third in his class and hopes to finish the year in first place, and says his favourite subject is Arabic.

He said he would rather be back in a regular school building with tables and chairs, rather than a tent like his home, but is ready for a new school year with notebooks, books and stationery provided by aid groups.

“But what can we do? It’s OK. The important thing is that we study,” he said. “I’m excited for this school year. I hope it continues without any problems.”

Like Osama, many children are still studying in tents and other temporary learning spaces, with cramped conditions and limited resources, UNICEF said.

It is far from a normal school environment and this situation can be seen at Ahbab Shujayea School, a makeshift school housed in worn-out tents near Gaza City’s port area.

School supplies, including basic items such as notebooks and pencils, have been banned from entering Gaza during the war. While some restrictions have been lifted, Palestinian authorities said just this month that Israel had prevented a shipment of school bags and stationery from UNICEF from entering the enclave.

At this school, there are no desks or chairs, so first and second-grade students sit crowded together on the ground, using pieces of cardboard to write on. Their teacher, who also has little to work with, explains the lesson on a very small board.

The school’s director, Inaam al-Batreekhi, said this was the best they could provide the children, given the circumstances.

“More than 300 students are enrolled at Ahbab Shujayea School, but unfortunately, they are students without notebooks or stationery,” al-Batreekhi told Al Jazeera.

“We can study today, we can sit on the ground today. But tomorrow, when the rain comes, we won’t be able to.”

The school serves children from nine displacement camps around the port, from first to sixth grade. Due to security concerns, such as Israeli shelling from the sea, the school day has been shortened, with classes running from 8am to 11am.

“Sometimes students come late and tell me, ‘I was filling water for my mother,’” al-Batreekhi said. “These are displaced children. A short while ago, they were carrying water and food. Now they are here trying to learn.”

She runs the school voluntarily and her ambition is for classes to return to a proper building.

“I hope we can return to official schools, to buildings. All the buildings are gone. All the schools have become tents,” she said. “In previous wars, we would miss school for a month or two, then return and find our school as it was. We would clean it, organise it and go back to studying. Now, returning to schools like that is almost impossible in the blink of an eye.”

For now, al-Batreekhi says the priority is to make this temporary school as comfortable as possible for the children.

“I hope the situation at the school and for the students will improve, and that we can get the support we need to improve their learning conditions,” she said.

“Even having chairs and desks would make a difference. These are children in first and second grade, and they are just beginning their education. They deserve to have the basic conditions to learn.”

articles.title: Will Trump’s new divide-and-conquer plan work against universities?
articles.summary: Every college and university should agree on one issue MacMahon did not explicitly address: the United States government should never condition research funding or other benefits on adherence to the political agenda of this or any other administration.
articles.body:
Last fall, the Trump administration offered a deal to nine of the nation’s top universities. They could either sign a 10-page compact accepting administration priorities and receive preferential access to federal funding, or they could decline and forgo federal benefits.

The administration hoped to extend the compact to all colleges and universities. Instead, its blatant attempt to dictate university policies helped convince all nine universities to refuse it.

Today, the administration is trying a subtler approach. Last month, Education Secretary Linda MacMahon issued what she called a “ national call to action ” asking every college and university to explain how it will ensure merit-based admissions, promote viewpoint diversity, stop protests from disrupting classes, make education affordable, support workforce needs, end grade inflation, and resist foreign influence.

MacMahon’s call to action may get traction, we fear, because it invites colleges and universities to divide themselves into two groups, the cooperative and the recalcitrant.

Although MacMahon’s letter does not contain an explicit quid pro quo, a White House official acknowledged that institutions that implement reforms “could be more likely to be involved in discussions” about reshaping federal research funding. How subtle.

Accountability in MacMahon’s Department of Education apparently means political control. It seems likely that MacMahon’s new approach will increase the fragmentation of higher education, making it even more difficult for colleges and universities to resist the administration’s attacks on everything from merit-based research funding to universities’ tax-exempt status.

To develop its call to action, the administration consulted a range of higher education leaders. Barbara Snyder, president of the Association of American Universities, described the discussions as an “ olive branch .” Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education, insisted that “unlike the compact, which was a gun-to-the-head ultimatum ,” MacMahon’s letter was “an invitation to a conversation.”

PEN America and the Alliance for Higher Education saw something more ominous — “a document designed to divide and weaken higher education.” And the American Federation of Teachers and the American Association of University Professors urged “organized resistance — not preemptive compliance” with what they viewed as another effort to undermine the ability of colleges and universities to govern themselves and impose the administration’s “far-right agenda” on them.

Most colleges and universities have so far remained noncommittal or silent. But the University of North Carolina system endorsed MacMahon’s approach and detailed its efforts to address her concerns, while all 40 presidents of Florida’s public colleges and universities signed a 30-page joint letter praising the call to action and answering its questions. Florida Education Commissioner Henry Mack demanded the state’s private universities respond as well.

Although Trump administration officials insist participation is voluntary, Mack made clear that in Florida, “institutions that ignore Secretary McMahon’s call to action, or that offer only empty rhetoric, should not be surprised by additional statutory requirements, tighter performance expectations, heightened scrutiny of licensure conditions or funding determinations calibrated to demonstrate seriousness.” McMahon praised Florida for “setting a bold example in answering our call to action — committing to commonsense reforms.”

In less than three weeks, a nominally voluntary federal invitation became, in the Sunshine State, a mandate backed by threats of state sanctions.

Florida may prove to be a model for others. Many red states have already passed legislation aligned with administration goals on diversity, equity and inclusion, faculty governance, curriculum, tenure and institutional authority. And the Heritage Foundation simultaneously offered states a blueprint in the form of model legislation for enacting administration priorities into law. Among other things, it would allow states to condition funding on compliance with prescribed policies on admissions, “identity-based activities,” viewpoint diversity and immigration enforcement. It would also subject universities to periodic “rights audits” and require review of academic programs for possible consolidation or elimination.

In short, MacMahon’s approach is generating what the original compact could not: a spectrum of responses, from enthusiastic endorsement to cautious engagement to silence, rather than nearly unanimous resistance.

Colleges and universities have until Dec. 31 to decide whether and how to respond. Between now and then, every institution that embraces MacMahon’s agenda provides an example federal and state officials can use to pressure those that object.

We believe that the questions MacMahon asks about existing policies are legitimate even if the answers she seeks are not. Universities should worry about affordability, grade inflation, academic rigor, free expression and foreign interference; they should enact reforms they independently decide are warranted. That makes her call to action hard to ignore and harder still to produce a shared response to it.

At a minimum, however, every college and university should agree on one issue MacMahon did not explicitly address: the U.S. government should never condition research funding or other benefits on adherence to the political agenda of this or any other administration.

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

articles.title: Pass the Protect College Sports Act
articles.summary: To preserve the unique commercial and educational model of intercollegiate athletics amidst numerous legal challenges, Matthew Mitten argues that Congress should pass the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act.
articles.body:
College sports are at a crossroads. The uniquely American and very popular national system of athletic competition between college student athletes, which has flourished for more than a century, is currently under assault by almost 150 federal and state lawsuits challenging various NCAA rules that maintain it.

Congress should enact the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act to protect the current commercial-educational model of intercollegiate sports, which differs from the commercial-professional model for pro sports.

Each major professional league has privately owned for-profit member clubs that produce the highest level of U.S. competition in a single sport (for example, the NBA and WNBA; the NFL), whose players are unionized club employees.

In contrast, the NCAA has 1,075 nonprofit member four-year colleges and universities in three nationwide divisions and subdivisions, which have significantly varying levels of athletic competition and resources. NCAA schools produce 24 intercollegiate sports with more than 90 men’s, women’s, and coed divisional national championship competitions.

Unlike NBA, NFL and WNBA players, NCAA athletes are full-time undergraduate or graduate students who must satisfy minimum NCAA and institutional academic requirements to participate in intercollegiate sports.

During 2024-25, NCAA schools fielded approximately 20,000 teams providing 554,298 intercollegiate sports participation opportunities for female and male student athletes. Division I men’s basketball and FBS football historically are the only sports generating surplus revenues, which cross-subsidize the costs of producing other intercollegiate sports, including women’s and Olympic sports. Less than 3 percent of NCAA university athletic departments generate annual revenues exceeding their expenses; all are Division I FBS Power Four conference (ACC, Big Ten, Big 12 and SEC) schools.

After college, less than 2 percent of NCAA intercollegiate athletes play their sport professionally.

Since the NCAA’s 1906 founding, more than 5 million men and women have played a wide variety of intercollegiate sports, providing each with the opportunity to earn a college degree. Historically, student athletes’ graduation rates are higher than the general student body at their respective educational institutions, but likely will decline if they continue transferring schools several times, as has occurred in recent years.

The Protect College Sports Act preserves the college sports commercial/educational model by providing that only a “student athlete” satisfying required academic standards and not a “professional athlete” is eligible to participate in intercollegiate athletics for a maximum of five years and generally must be 24 years of age or younger. It would maintain or increase student athlete graduation rates by generally permitting only one institutional transfer without losing or delaying eligibility to participate in intercollegiate sports.

The Protect College Sports Act provides important educational protections for student athletes by prohibiting athletic department pressure regarding their selection of courses or majors, or the reduction or revocation of an athletic scholarship because of athletic performance or injury, with a private right of action for violations. It requires Division I schools to continue providing their former student-athletes with financial educational assistance equal to the value of their individual athletic scholarships for 10 years after expiration of intercollegiate sports eligibility.

The Protect College Sports Act establishes a nationally uniform law permitting all intercollegiate athletes to earn compensation for the commercial use of their individual Name, Image, and Likeness rights and preempts the current hodgepodge of more than 30 conflicting state college laws. It requires disclosure of student-athlete compensation over $600 per year; prohibits non-university “pay-for-play” Name, Image and Likeness agreements with student-athletes that exceed the fair market value of a comparable non-college athlete product or service endorsement contract; and provides antitrust immunity for NCAA, conference, and schools’ enforcement of these requirements.

Pursuant to the House antitrust settlement and beginning in July 2025, NCAA Division I athletes may receive individualized payments from their respective universities, initially aggregating up to $20.5 million per school annually and increasing each year ($21.3 million for 2026-27) to an estimated $32.9 million per school cap in 2034-35.

The Protect College Sports Act legislatively approves the House annual revenue sharing cap (extending its duration with annual inflation adjustments), prohibits its circumvention, and immunizes its terms and enforcement from future antitrust challenge.

This proposed federal law permits a Division I university to exceed this general revenue sharing cap up to an additional $22.5 million per year to retain its own current intercollegiate athletes and an additional $5 million per year for its women’s, Olympic, and other non-revenue sports athletes.

In addition to protecting the college sports commercial/educational model, the Protect College Sports Act promotes on-field competitive balance by establishing nationally uniform college athlete eligibility and compensation rules; protects its integrity by permitting enforcement of college athlete sports gambling and doping prohibitions; and permits internal governance of intercollegiate athletics consistent with the legitimate objectives of higher education and national public interest.

The future of college athletics should not be uncertain because of conflicting state laws and judicial micromanaging. Congress should stabilize intercollegiate sports by enacting the Protect College Sports Act.

Matthew Mitten is professor of law and senior advisor at Marquette University Law School’s National Sports Law Institute.
